paragraphs: “The air out here is fresh, but in my apartment it isn’t, in any sense of the word. Let’s walk slowly, sir. I would be glad of your kind attention.”
“I have something important to say to you too,” said Alyosha, “only I don’t know how to begin.”

“Of course you must have business with me. You wouldn’t have looked in on me without some purpose. Unless you’ve come simply to complain about the boy, and that’s hardly likely. And by the way, about the boy: I couldn’t explain to you in there, but out here I’ll describe that scene to you. My tow was thicker a week ago—I mean my beard. That’s the nickname they give my beard, the schoolboys most of all. Well, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch was pulling me by my beard. I’d done nothing; he was in a towering rage and happened to run into me. He dragged me out of the tavern into the market-place. At that moment the boys were coming out of school, and Ilusha was with them. As soon as he saw me in that state, he rushed up to me. ‘Father,’ he cried, ‘father!’ He caught hold of me, hugged me, tried to pull me away, and shouted to the man who was attacking me, ‘Let go, let go, it’s my father, forgive him!’—yes, he actually cried ‘forgive him.’ He clutched at that hand, that very hand, in his little hands and kissed it.... I remember his little face at that moment. I haven’t forgotten it and I never will!”

“I swear,” cried Alyosha, “that my brother will express his deepest and most sincere regret, even if he has to go down on his knees in that same market-place.... I’ll make him do it, or he is no brother of mine!”

“Aha, so it’s only a suggestion! And it doesn’t come from him, but simply from the generosity of your own warm heart. You should have said so. No, in that case let me tell you about your brother’s highly chivalrous, soldierly generosity, for he did show it at the time. He stopped dragging me by my beard and let me go. ‘You are an officer,’ he said, ‘and I am an officer. If you can find a decent man to be your second, send me your challenge. I will give you satisfaction, though you are a scoundrel.’ That’s what he said. A chivalrous spirit indeed! I left with Ilusha, and that scene is a family record, stamped forever on Ilusha’s soul. No, it’s not for us to claim the privileges of noblemen. Judge for yourself. You’ve just been in our mansion. What did you see there? Three ladies: one a cripple and weak-minded, another a cripple and a hunchback, and the third not crippled but far too clever. She is a student, dying to get back to Petersburg, to work for the emancipation of the Russian woman on the banks of the Neva. I won’t speak of Ilusha; he is only nine. I am alone in the world, and if I die, what will become of all of them? That’s all I ask you. And if I challenge him and he kills me on the spot, what then? What will become of them? And worse still, if he doesn’t kill me but only cripples me: I couldn’t work, but I would still be a mouth to feed. Who would feed me, and who would feed them all? Must I take Ilusha out of school and send him to beg in the streets? That’s what it means for me to challenge him to a duel. It’s silly talk and nothing else.”
“He will beg your forgiveness. He will bow down at your feet in the middle of the market-place,” cried Alyosha again, with glowing eyes.

“I did think of taking him to court,” the captain went on, “but look in our code: could I get much compensation for a personal injury? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna[3] sent for me and shouted at me: ‘Don’t you dare dream of it! If you go after him, I’ll tell the whole world that he beat you for your dishonesty, and then you’ll be prosecuted.’ I call God to witness whose dishonesty it was and on whose orders I acted. Wasn’t it on her own and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? ‘And what’s more,’ she went on, ‘I’ll dismiss you for good, and you’ll never earn another penny from me. I’ll speak to my merchant too’ (that’s what she calls her old man) ‘and he will dismiss you!’ And if he dismisses me, what can I earn then, from anyone? Those two are all I have to look to, because your Fyodor Pavlovitch has not only stopped employing me, for another reason, but he means to use papers I’ve signed to take me to court. And so I kept quiet, and you have seen our retreat. But now let me ask you: did Ilusha hurt your finger much? I didn’t like to go into it in our mansion, in front of him.”

“Yes, very much, and he was in a great fury. He was taking revenge on me for you, as a Karamazov. I see that now. But if only you had seen how he was throwing stones at his schoolmates! It’s very dangerous. They might kill him. They are children, and stupid. A stone can be thrown and break somebody’s head.”
“That’s just what has happened. He was hit by a stone today. Not on the head but on the chest, just above the heart. He came home crying and groaning, and now he is ill.”
“And you know, he attacks them first. He is bitter against them on your account. They say he stabbed a boy called Krassotkin with a penknife not long ago.”
“I’ve heard about that too. It’s dangerous. Krassotkin is an official here; we may hear more about it.”
“I would advise you,” Alyosha went on warmly, “not to send him to school at all for a while, until he is calmer ... and his anger has passed.”

“Anger!” the captain repeated. “That’s just what it is. He is a little creature, but it’s a mighty anger. You don’t know all of it, sir. Let me tell you more. Since that incident all the boys have been teasing him about the ‘wisp of tow.’ Schoolboys are a merciless race. Individually they are angels, but together, especially in schools, they are often merciless. Their teasing has stirred up a gallant spirit in Ilusha. An ordinary boy, a weak son, would have given in and felt ashamed of his father, sir. But he stood up for his father against them all. For his father, and for truth and justice. What he suffered when he kissed your brother’s hand and cried to him ‘Forgive father, forgive him’—only God knows that, and I, his father. Our children—not your children, but ours, the children of poor gentlemen looked down on by everyone—know what justice means, sir, even at nine years old. How would the rich know? They don’t explore such depths once in their lives. But at that moment in the square when he kissed his hand, at that moment my Ilusha had grasped everything that justice means. That truth went into him and crushed him forever, sir,” the captain said hotly again, with a kind of frenzy, and he struck his right fist against his left palm, as though to show how “the truth” crushed Ilusha. “That very day, sir, he fell ill with fever and was delirious all night. All that day he hardly said a word to me, but I noticed he kept watching me from the corner, though he turned to the window and pretended to be learning his lessons. I could see his mind was not on his lessons. The next day I got drunk to forget my troubles, sinful man that I am, and I don’t remember much. Mamma began crying, too—I am very fond of mamma—well, I spent my last penny drowning my troubles. Don’t despise me for that, sir. In Russia the men who drink are the best. The best men among us are the greatest drunkards. I lay down and I don’t remember anything about Ilusha, though all that day the boys had been jeering at him at school. ‘Wisp of tow,’ they shouted, ‘your father was dragged out of the tavern by his wisp of tow, and you ran after him and begged forgiveness.’”

“On the third day, when he came back from school, I saw he looked pale and wretched. ‘What is it?’ I asked. He wouldn’t answer. Well, there’s no talking in our mansion without mamma and the girls taking part. What’s more, the girls had heard about it the very first day. Varvara had begun snarling: ‘You fools and buffoons, can you ever do anything sensible?’ ‘Quite so,’ I said, ‘can we ever do anything sensible?’ For the time being I turned it off like that. So in the evening I took the boy out for a walk, because, you must know, we go for a walk every evening, always the same way, the way we are going now—from our gate to that big stone which lies alone in the road under the hurdle, where the town pasture begins. A beautiful, lonely spot, sir. Ilusha and I walked along hand in hand as usual. He has a little hand, his fingers are thin and cold—he suffers with his chest, you know. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father!’ ‘Well?’ said I. I saw his eyes flashing. ‘Father, how he treated you then!’ ‘It can’t be helped, Ilusha,’ I said. ‘Don’t forgive him, father, don’t forgive him! At school they say he paid you ten roubles for it.’ ‘No, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘I wouldn’t take money from him for anything.’ Then he began trembling all over, took my hand in both of his and kissed it again. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father, challenge him to a duel. At school they say you’re a coward and won’t challenge him, and that you’ll accept ten roubles from him.’ ‘I can’t challenge him to a duel, Ilusha,’ I answered. And I told him briefly what I’ve just told you. He listened. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘anyway, don’t forgive it. When I grow up, I’ll call him out myself and kill him.’ His eyes shone and glowed. And of course I am his father, and I had to put in a word: ‘It’s a sin to kill,’ I said, ‘even in a duel.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘when I grow up, I’ll knock him down, knock the sword out of his hand, fall on him, wave my sword over him and say: “I could kill you, but I forgive you, so there!”’ You see what has been going on in his little mind these two days. He must have been planning that revenge all day, and raving about it at night.

“But he began to come home from school badly beaten. I found out about it the day before yesterday, and you are right, I won’t send him to that school any more. I heard that he was standing up against the whole class alone and defying them all, that his heart was full of resentment and bitterness—I was alarmed about him. We went for another walk. ‘Father,’ he asked, ‘are the rich stronger than anyone else on earth?’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘there are no people on earth stronger than the rich.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘I will get rich, I will become an officer and conquer everybody. The Tsar will reward me, I will come back here and then no one will dare—’ Then he was silent, and his lips still kept trembling. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘what a horrid town this is.’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘it isn’t a very nice town.’ ‘Father, let’s move to another town, a nice one,’ he said, ‘where people don’t know about us.’ ‘We will move, we will, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘only I must save up for it.’ I was glad to be able to turn his mind from painful thoughts, and we began to dream of how we would move to another town, how we would buy a horse and cart. ‘We’ll put mamma and your sisters inside and cover them up, and we’ll walk. You’ll get a lift now and then, and I’ll walk beside you, because we must take care of our horse. We can’t all ride. That’s how we’ll go.’ He was enchanted by that, most of all by the thought of having a horse and driving it. For of course a Russian boy is born among horses. We chattered for a long while. Thank God, I thought, I have taken his mind off it and comforted him.

“That was the day before yesterday, in the evening, but last night everything changed. He had gone to school in the morning and came back depressed, terribly depressed. In the evening I took him by the hand and we went for a walk, but he wouldn’t talk. There was a wind blowing and no sun, and a feeling of autumn; twilight was coming on. We walked along, both of us depressed. ‘Well, my boy,’ said I, ‘how about setting off on our travels?’ I thought I might bring him back to our talk of the day before. He didn’t answer, but I felt his fingers trembling in my hand. Ah, I thought, it’s a bad business; there’s something new. We had reached the stone where we are now. I sat down on the stone. And in the air there were lots of kites flapping and whirling. There were as many as thirty in sight. Of course, it’s just the season for kites. ‘Look, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘it’s time we got out last year’s kite again. I’ll mend it. Where have you put it away?’ My boy made no answer. He looked away and turned sideways to me. And then a gust of wind blew up the sand. He suddenly fell on me, threw both his little arms around my neck and held me tight. You know, when children are silent and proud, and try to hold back their tears when they are in great trouble, and then suddenly break down, their tears fall in streams. With those warm streams of tears he suddenly wet my face. He sobbed and shook as though he were in convulsions, and squeezed up against me as I sat on the stone. ‘Father,’ he kept crying, ‘dear father, how he insulted you!’ And I sobbed too. We sat shaking in each other’s arms. ‘Ilusha,’ I said to him, ‘Ilusha darling.’ No one saw us then. God alone saw us. I hope He will record it to my credit. You must thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. No, sir, I won’t thrash my boy for your satisfaction.”
